# The Beating

Margarete had been tuning pianos for fifty-one years, and she could hear disagreement anywhere.

Not metaphorical disagreement—the literal kind, the kind measured in cents and hertz. When two strings meant to speak as one drifted apart even slightly, they fought, producing a third sound that belonged to neither of them: a slow pulse, a wavering, a beating. Far apart, the beat was frantic, urgent as a trapped bird. Drawn closer, it slowed, calmed, stretched into longer silences between pulses, until at last the two tones merged and the beating stopped entirely.

Her work was to listen for the fighting, and to end it.

She'd learned this from her father, who had learned it in a factory in Leipzig, though he never talked about the factory, only about the ears the work required—not good ears, he insisted, patient ones. Any child can hear that a note is wrong. The craft was in hearing *how* wrong, and in which direction. You struck two keys and listened to the space between them fill with that trembling pulse. Then you reached into the piano with your mute wedge and your tuning lever and coaxed one string toward the other, and the beat slowed, slowed, stopped—and for a moment the note was not two things agreeing but one thing, indivisible, complete.

Fifty-one years of Tuesdays and Thursdays in strangers' living rooms. She had learned to read households by their pianos: the upright in the parsonage, pocked with hymnal stickers; the baby grand nobody played, lid closed like a held breath, one string dead because a pencil had fallen inside decades ago and been chewed to splinters by hammers; the school practice rooms with their scarred fallboards; the concert hall, where she worked alone at midnight before every season, the building humming around her like a sleeping animal while she moved through it with lamp and tools, a small priest tending a large god.

People assumed tuning was about making notes correct. It wasn't. Correct was impossible—a piano tuned to pure intervals sounded worse, not better; the mathematics refused to cooperate; the circle wouldn't close. So tuners compromised. They stretched the octaves slightly wide, narrowed the fifths, distributed the error so evenly that no single interval confessed. Equal temperament, it was called: a system of beautiful lies arranged so carefully that the ear forgave them all. Every note on the keyboard was wrong on purpose, and wrong in just the right way, so that music could travel anywhere without breaking.

Her father had explained it once, hands spread on the kitchen table. *You cannot make everyone happy,* he said. *You make no one too unhappy.*

She had been thinking about that lately, in the evenings, in the apartment that still smelled faintly of rosin and wool. She was eighty now. Her left hand trembled on cold mornings, and the tuning lever demanded a steadiness she could no longer always promise. She had trained apprentices, most of whom left for steadier trades. One remained: Daniel, twenty-six, who wore headphones around his neck in restaurants and heard everything anyway.

Last month she took him to a job she might once have declined. A hospice, a common room, an old upright the staff wanted working because a dying woman had asked whether anyone could fix the piano, and the staff had decided that anything within their power should probably be done.

The instrument was terrible. Water damage along the base, rust blooming on the strings like orange lichen. Daniel looked at her with the question already on his face, but she was kneeling, pressing keys one by one, cataloguing casualties. Three dead strings. Two others wild. The rest merely exhausted, flattened by years, speaking a semitone shy of their intentions.

They worked through the afternoon. He replaced what could be replaced; she tuned what could be tuned. When they finished, the piano was not good—it would never be good again—but it was honest. Every key spoke. Nothing lied about what it was.

The woman came down in her wheelchair after dinner. She had been a music teacher, someone said. Her hands were swollen, knuckles like river stones, and she could manage only a few chords, the beginnings of songs everyone knew. She played them slowly, over and over, sometimes stopping mid-phrase as if she'd forgotten why she'd started. No one sang. The staff pretended to do paperwork. Margarete sat by the window with her coat still on, not leaving yet.

And there it was, she thought. This was what the work was for. Not the concert hall, not the perfect unison, not the vanished beating. This: a broken instrument made barely sufficient, and a pair of ruined hands finding in it exactly enough music to mean something.

On the drive home Daniel said, "It was really far gone. We probably shouldn't have charged them."

"We didn't," she said.

He nodded, drumming the wheel at a red light, and she watched him and thought about beats again—how two voices near each other produce that pulse, that trembling argument, and how you spend a lifetime learning to bring them together. But maybe she had it backward. Maybe the beating wasn't the flaw. Maybe it was how you knew both voices were alive. Perfect silence between tones is death; perfect agreement is only another name for one thing gone. The world runs on slight differences, on near-misses and almosts, on two people in a room playing nearly the same note.

At her door, Daniel carried her tools upstairs, and she let him. Inside, she didn't turn on lights. She stood in the dark kitchen, eighty years old, ears still patient, and listened to the building settle around her: pipes ticking, the refrigerator humming a flat B, the radiator knocking its arrhythmic code. Nothing in tune. Everything speaking.

She put the kettle on and let the evening beat against her—softly, softly, like a heart deciding to continue.
